text:
maria: quick heads-up — ran a long nsys capture against the kv-cache repro and noticed two distinct CUDA kernels (small GEMM + kv-apply) collapsed into what looks like a single long kernel on the timeline. feels like sparse sampling merged them, making the hotspot analysis misleading.

alex: can you paste the exact nsys command you used? also which trace set?

maria: ran something like:
```
nsys profile -o trace_kv --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --duration=20 ./bin/serve_repro --cfg small-batch
```
no explicit sample flags, default capture.

jonas: default sampling can miss short gaps and OSRT markers if the sample window is too coarse. do you have NVTX ranges around the two phases? without NVTX nsys might attribute them to the same cuda kernel if the GPU work is interleaved rapidly.

maria: i didn't NVTX them the first run. added NVTX in the repro:
```
NVTX_RANGE_PUSH("kv-apply"); kv_apply(...); NVTX_RANGE_POP();
NVTX_RANGE_PUSH("small-gemm"); run_gemm(...); NVTX_RANGE_POP();
```
that made them separate in a follow-up trace.

alex: nice. two quick suggestions: 1) capture with --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt (you already do) but also bump sampling granularity / duration so the profiler sees the transition edges; 2) try bracketed capture so you avoid startup noise: start/stop around the steady-state segment.

jonas: append to alex's tip — when you increase sampling granularity, you can also rely less on stack sampling and more on NVTX for attribution. NVTX gives deterministic ranges and will show the split even if the sampler only catches a fraction of events.

maria: tried:
```
nsys profile -o trace_kv_nvtx --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --duration=25 --sample=1us ./bin/serve_repro --cfg small-batch
```
that made the timeline denser and the two kernels look distinct, but i also saw a repeated pattern where the kernel launcher merged small launches into a contiguous execution window — looks like command queueing on the GPU.

alex: queueing / kernel coalescing is real. OS-side batching and driver reordering can pack launches closely enough to look like one long kernel. a couple of heuristics to probe this: add a tiny cudaStreamSynchronize between phases in the repro to force separation, or toggle stream affinity so launches land in separate streams to see if the timeline splits.

jonas: also try capture-range using NVTX or API markers to avoid pre/post noise:
```
nsys profile -o out --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --capture-range=nvtx:start_marker:end_marker --duration=15 ./bin/serve_repro
```
that way the capture is precisely the segment of interest.

maria: good tip — used NVTX bracket markers and a 15s capture, kernel split is visible and attribution improved. one weird artifact remains: the per-kernel elapsed time in the CUDA table still reports a single long duration for the merged region, even though NVTX shows two ranges. feels like the underlying CUPTI records a single device-side kernel.

alex: yep, CUPTI/device-side reports kernel durations as the device saw them. if small kernels are actually launched as a fused or persistent-kernel on device (driver-level fusion or persistent worker patterns), CUPTI won't split them. NVTX is a host annotation only. for true device splitting you'd need per-kernel nvprof/CUPTI hooks or instrument at the dispatch source.

jonas: actionable checklist:
- add NVTX ranges around kv and gemm (done)
- try forcing stream/sync to test queueing vs fusion
- run with bracketed capture (--capture-range=nvtx) to reduce noise
- increase sampling density/duration for timeline fidelity
- if device-reported durations still merged, add a lightweight kernel counter (atomic increments at dispatch) or enable CUPTI callbacks to see per-launch records

maria: filing a short PR for NVTX ranges and a repro script that toggles stream sync. i'll also add a CI nsys smoke that runs a tiny bracketed trace and uploads a short nsys summary artifact.

ci-bot: created task INF-813: "nsys repro: kv-cache kernel-split hypothesis + NVTX" assigned to maria. :white_check_mark:

alex: perfect. once we have the CI smoke we can iterate on sampling params and document a short playbook for triaging merged-kernel symptoms (sampling sparsity vs driver coalescing vs device fusion).

maria: thanks — will paste the minimal script and a couple of example captures into the ticket.

jonas: one last note — when you paste commands in the ticket, include the nsys CLI output summary (rep file size, interval counts). those numbers make it easier to reason about sampling coverage.
